Necessity compelling, an art was finally invented by which he might pay the penalty for so much blood. The narrow paths of the trails by which he was accustomed to go out at night from the shelters of the caves for prey were explored, and the path was cut. They excavated a pit and covered it with hurdles and thrown earth, the excess soil having been dispersed. <margin>What about the tiger?</margin> When the unsuspecting male tiger came, he fell into the pit and became fixed upon sharp stakes set in the bottom of the pit. With his roaring, he deafened the whole neighborhood, and the mountains echoed with that shrieking. He was killed by huge stones thrown onto him from the edges of the ditch, and by the stakes already fixed in him. He broke the spears aimed and thrown from above into a thousand fragments and a thousand splinters. While half-dead and drained of blood, he still filled those watching with terror, considering what he might have done had he been loose and unharmed. A certain Juan de Ledesma, a man from Seville, a friend and companion in labors of Vasco, confessed that he had eaten of that tiger. He reported to me that it was no worse than beef. When asked, those who saw the tiger where they might say it is a tiger, they reply that they judge it to be a tiger from the spots, from its ferocity, from its dexterity, and from other signs given by the authors, although many of them claim to have seen spotted leopards and panthers themselves. After the tiger was killed, they followed his tracks toward the mountains and reached his den, his conjugal dwelling.

In the absence of the mother, they took two cubs, not yet ready to be weaned. Having changed their plan to send them to Spain once they were grown, they returned the little ones to the mother's den, with iron chains carefully fastened around their necks. Returning to the cave a few days later, they found the cave empty, with the chains exactly where they had left them. They thought the mother had torn them to pieces out of rage and carried them off, so that no one might enjoy them. For they assert that they could by no means have freed themselves alive from the chains. The skin of the killed tiger was sent to Hispaniola, stuffed with dry herbs and straw, to the Admiral and the leaders from whom these laws and aid for the new lands are expected. And those who suffered inconveniences from the tiger, and those who handled his skin, explained these things to me, which I record as received. One must return to Pacra, from whom we had digressed. Vasco entered the houses—that is, the <term>boios</term> <gloss>dwellings</gloss>—of Pacra, and he endeavored to draw Pacra out. Through <margin>Pacra returns.</margin> envoys, he signified the same things to Pacra that we have mentioned were signified to the others. For a long time, Pacra refused. Threats were added to the refusal. He finally came, accompanied by three chieftains. Vasco writes that Pacra was so deformed, so filthy, and so foul that he confesses he had never seen anything more hideous. He says that nature had granted him only a human <margin>What sort of man is Pacra? He is held as a monster.</margin> form; otherwise, he was a brute, wild animal, monstrous. His character, he says, was equal to his habits and features. He was abusing the daughters of four neighboring chieftains whom he had taken by force with detestable lust. Many things regarding the obscene character of Pacra and other such infinite things were cast before Vasco by the neighboring chieftains as if before a praetorian judge, or Hercules the avenger, so that punishment might be taken upon Pacra. The beast, along with the three chieftains who obeyed Pacra's command and suffered from the same <margin>What is done against the wicked.</margin> sicknesses, he threw to the jaws of the war dogs, and he ordered their lacerated corpses to be burned. Regarding the dogs with whom they engage in battle, amazing things are reported. Against armed natives, it is not a fierce contest; there was no need for swords or arrows or other weapons to rout the opposing enemies. For once the signal was given and the dogs were released, the column, terrified by the appearance and unusual barking of the Molossian dogs, would hesitate and, in <margin>Amazing things about the dogs.</margin> confusion, abandon their battle lines and orders. It happens differently, however, when they engage with the Caramairenses and Caribs; for they are fiercer and more apt at waging wars. Charging, they aim their poisoned arrows at the dogs, just as if they had been struck by lightning, and kill many. The inhabitants of these mountains, however, do not wage war with arrows; they use only <term>machanae</term> <gloss>broad, oblong wooden swords</gloss> and javelins and fire-hardened spears against their enemies. <margin>With what weapons they wage war.</margin> From the living Pacra, where his family members collected gold could never be extorted by any enticements, threats, or tortures. When asked where he had that—for thirty pounds of gold had been taken from his treasury—he answered that his family members who used to collect gold from those mountains in the time of his parents and his own were dead. He had had no concern since he passed puberty for searching for gold. He could never be pulled from this proposed institution. <margin>30 pounds of gold from Pacra.</margin> From this severity toward Pacra, Vasco reconciled the minds of the neighboring chieftains to himself. <summary>This page details the capture and death of a tiger-like predator and describes the harsh judgment Vasco imposed upon the chieftain Pacra, including the use of war dogs to execute him and his associates.</summary>
